notes:
These notes cover 1 Chronicles 1:1–27. Each point is followed by the page it came from.

**Overview (vv. 1–27)**
- Guzik: the chronicler leaves out Cain and Abel and names only Seth, which shows he was inspired by God to make a selective genealogy for a specific purpose. He also says the lists mattered to the returning exiles because they showed God's work carrying on through the generations and helped them see their own place in it. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/
- Precept Austin: because the chapter starts with Adam rather than Abraham, it shows that the God of Israel is the Creator and Lord of the whole world, not just of one nation. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary
- Corduan (Gospel Coalition) thinks Ezra wrote it. His reason for starting with Adam is that in the final analysis we are all the offspring of the same man, namely Adam. https://www.thegospelcoalition.org/commentary/1-chronicles/
- Matthew Henry: the section starts with Adam and ends with Abraham. Adam was the common father of our flesh, Abraham the common father of the faithful. Verses 1–4 and 24–27 together form Christ's line, which Luke 3:34–38 repeats in reverse order. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-27.html

**v. 1**
- Gill: verses 1–4 match Genesis 5 exactly. In the Hebrew the first letter of "Adam" is written larger than usual, as a memorial of the first man. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-1.htm
- Clarke (Methodist): Cain and Abel are skipped because the writer only wanted the one line from Adam to Noah, and Noah did not descend from either of them. https://www.studylight.org/bible/eng/net/1-chronicles/1-1.html
- Pulpit Commentary: the jump from Adam to Seth, ignoring Cain and Abel, is "full of suggestion." It also notes some hold that names have been left out of the list, which would mean the years are not complete either. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-1.htm
- Bible Hub study notes: Seth's name means "appointed" or "granted," and in Enosh's day people "men began to call upon the name of the LORD." https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/1-1.htm
- Ellicott (modern-scholarship angle): the Chaldeans also had a tradition of ten patriarchs before the Flood. He rejects the idea that the names are myth and calls such theories speculations that cannot possibly be verified. https://biblehub.com/1_chronicles/1-1.htm

**vv. 2–3**
- Precept Austin: the line from Adam continues through godly Seth. Enoch is remembered above all because he "walked with God" (Genesis 5:24). https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary

**v. 4**
- Guzik: Noah and his three sons, all survivors of the Flood, became the basis of the nations after the Flood. The line from Adam to Noah belongs to all humanity. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/
- Gill: Shem's family is listed last because Abraham and then the Messiah came from his line. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-17.htm

**vv. 5–7**
- Guzik, citing Payne: Japheth's sons are commonly thought to have founded the peoples of Europe and northern Asia. Javan is linked to Greek Ionia, Gomer to the Cimmerians, Madai to the Medes, and Tubal and Meshech to the Turkish plateau. The Kittites and Rodanites are Cyprus and Rhodes. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/
- Keil and Delitzsch: small spelling differences from Genesis 10 (for example Diphath and Riphath) are partly just spelling and partly copying errors. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-10.htm

**vv. 8–9**
- Guzik: Mizraim is Egypt and Put is Libya. Cush seems to have split into two branches, one tied to Babylon and one to Ethiopia. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/
- Precept Austin: Raamah's sons Sheba and Dedan became linked with Arabian trade routes and wealth. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary

**v. 10**
- Clarke quotes the Jewish Targum (an ancient Aramaic paraphrase), which says Nimrod "began to be bold in sin, a murderer of the innocent, and a rebel before the Lord." https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-10.html
- Matthew Henry: Nimrod began to be an oppressor, probably to the people of God in his time. The Geneva Bible's note (Calvinist) says he first lifted himself above others. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-10.html and https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-10.htm
- Precept Austin: Nimrod set up early centres of organised rebellion, including Babylon. Some link him with the "mighty men" (Nephilim) of Genesis 6:4 and think he was a giant, but Precept Austin calls that link untenable. https://www.preceptaustin.org/1-chronicles-1-commentary
- Cambridge Bible (critical view): Nimrod is tied to Babylonia and Assyria, yet verse 17 assigns those lands to Shem. It thinks the likelier explanation is that Nimrod's father Cush has been wrongly identified with Ham's son Cush. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-10.htm

**vv. 11–12**
- Guzik, citing Payne: the Philistines were "sea peoples" who came from the Casluhites. These were of Egyptian origin but related to Caphtor (Crete). https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/

**vv. 13–16**
- Guzik: Canaan stands for the peoples who first settled the land later known as Israel and the surrounding area. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/

**v. 17**
- Guzik: Elam is linked to the Persians, Asshur to the Assyrians, Lud to the Lydians and Aram to the Syrians. He notes that the list includes the nations that held Israel in exile, which reassured Israel that God's plan still included both them and those nations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/
- On Uz, Hul, Gether and Meshech appearing as Shem's "sons": Poole and Benson say "sons" can include grandsons. Keil and Delitzsch say the relationship to Aram is simply assumed to be known from Genesis. The Cambridge Bible (critical) thinks the words "and the sons of Aram" have dropped out of the Hebrew. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-17.htm
- Kretzmann (Lutheran) agrees that the last four are Aram's sons and Shem's grandsons. https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-1.html

**v. 18**
- Benson: Arphaxad fathered Shelah either directly or through an in-between son who appears in Luke 3:35. Benson's text names him "Canaan," but Luke 3:36 has Cainan. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-17.htm
- Guzik, citing Payne: "Eber" is the root of the word "Hebrew." https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/

**v. 19** (the commentators disagree most here)
- Mainstream view: the division at the tower of Babel. Guzik and Wesley (Methodist) take this view, and Wesley explains "divided" as In their languages and habitations. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/ and https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-19.html
- Ellicott: it probably refers to a split in the population of Mesopotamia. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-19.html
- A cyclopedia on StudyLight says it is usually taken as a split within Eber's own family, with Joktan's descendants moving to southern Arabia. https://www.studylight.org/encyclopedias/eng/mse/p/peleg.html
- Chuck Smith (Calvary Chapel) calls the meaning a matter of speculation. It could be Babel, though some think the continents were split apart. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-19.html
- A Bible Hub Q&A article argues for continental break-up in Peleg's lifetime, using young-earth "catastrophic plate tectonics." This is a disputed popular teaching. https://biblehub.com/q/Why_does_Peleg_s_name_mean_division.htm
- The Biblical Illustrator (sermon notes): God meant the earth to be divided peacefully, but sin turned the division into discord at Babel. https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-19.html

**vv. 20–23**
- Ellicott: Genesis 10:30 places Joktan's people from Mesha, at the head of the Persian Gulf, to south Arabia. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-17.htm
- Clarke rejects the idea that Jobab is Job, since the two names are not similar. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/

**vv. 24–27**
- Keil and Delitzsch: the names follow Genesis 11:10–26 but leave out the ages. Only Abram is named among Terah's sons, to point to the ancestor of the chosen people. https://biblehub.com/commentaries/1_chronicles/1-27.htm
- Kretzmann (Lutheran): the Lord himself changed Abram's name (Genesis 17:5). https://www.studylight.org/commentaries/eng/kpc/1-chronicles-1.html
- Matthew Henry urges readers to become Abraham's seed by faith (Romans 4:11–12). https://www.studylight.org/commentary/1-chronicles/1-27.html
- Guzik: God chose a Babylonian from a family that worshipped idols. https://enduringword.com/bible-commentary/1-chronicles-1/

**What I couldn't find**
- **Traditions:** I found no real disagreement between Protestant traditions in this passage. The Methodist (Wesley, Clarke), Lutheran (Kretzmann) and Calvinist (Geneva Bible) notes all read the genealogy the same basic way.
- **Catholic and Orthodox:** I didn't find any notes from newadvent.org, catholic.com or oca.org.
- **Modern scholarship:** I found no bibleodyssey.org or NET Bible notes. The only critical views are the Cambridge Bible's (vv. 10 and 17).
- **Other popular teaching:** Apart from the plate-tectonics reading of verse 19, I found nothing on prosperity, word-of-faith or hyper-grace teaching for these verses.
